utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Before we resume our proceedings, I would like to ask the Prosecution whether they turned over to the Defence the videotape about the Bungalow, the whole videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I believe we have. The videotape that was shown in court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: -- earlier? Yes. I believe we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. And we also, since the decision concerning the on-site visit to Ahmici has been circulated, we would welcome requests or comments from the parties in accordance with the Rules of Conduct. Point 5 states the parties will be asked in advance to request orally or in writing the points of the itinerary from where they would like to make observations relating to the Kupreskic trial. I wonder whether you could make such request today, so that we can decide how to proceed. All right. Now, the notes have been circulated, and I wonder whether the Defence counsel would like to continue with the cross-examination. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Lordship, this afternoon perhaps we shall be raising this question, but I should like you to allow each one of the Defence team to be allowed to say whether he has any objections or not. But would you like to do it now or shall we simply resume yesterday's work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, no, we should resume our work. I was asking about the notes taken by the witness which were distributed, and I wonder whether you had the opportunity to read those notes, and in light of those notes, to continue the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Lordship, yes, we have received those notes, and I should like to ask for your permission to begin with some other questions, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I proceed to the cross-examination, I should like to ask you for your attention and perhaps a little bit of patience. However, when I come to the end of this presentation, I believe you will understand why I have chosen this particular approach to this issue. Before I therefore start with the cross-examination, I should like to say a few words about another matter. Your Honours, yesterday the Prosecutor examined the witness, and the witness answered his questions about the murder of Samir Trako which happened in the Hotel Vitez in 1992. The witness says that he was prevented from conducting an investigation on site because Franjo Sucic was sent there upon the orders of Pero Skopljak, and the witness said that the scene of the crime had been tampered with meanwhile. Furthermore, the witness, when asked by the Prosecution, spoke about the events of the 2nd March, 1993, when Esad Salkic was murdered. He spoke about the brutal behaviour of a certain Miroslav Bralo, called Cicko. He also described the circumstances of that particular murder. The Prosecutor then directly examined the witness about the events on the 21st of October, 1992, when members of the BH army were killed, and the witness then also spoke about how they were treated by the Military Police which threw them out of the police vehicle in front of the police station in Stari Vitez, and then Vlado Santic intervened, and then things took another direction. Then the Prosecutor examined the witness about the events of the 26th of April, '93, in the Bungalow, and the witness said that they had been forced to get out of the van, put their hands up behind their heads, and so on and so forth, that is, the witness again spoke about the details of the event. The Prosecutor also examined the witness and the latter provided answers about certain conduct of Miroslav Bralo. Those people who happened to be in Kratine and who were allegedly digging trenches when this individual ill-treated them. Lastly, and this is important in this case, the Prosecutor asked the witness, and the witness answered accordingly, that he talked to Ivan Josipovic and Ivan Josipovic told him that Vlado Santic had taken an active part on the attack on the village of Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993, coming from the direction of the Bungalow. In other words, Your Lordships, I should like to warn that all that this witness answered was in direct questions from the Prosecutor, that is, it was not free statement, free testimony of the witness. When it came to the cross-examination and when I drew the attention of the Prosecutor that his questions did not all relate to the notes that were submitted to the Defence, the notes or, rather, the records of this witness on the 26th of July, '97, and when I drew attention to the fact that in the end it said that the witness's notes on ten pages were attached to it and that these notes were an integral part of this record, the Prosecutor said, you will remember, that he never noted, never saw those notes, and that he knew nothing about them. So that is one thing. I should also like to say another thing. I read those notes, and what does one see in them? On page 2 of the alleged notes of witness Zlotrg of the 5th of September, 1996, one can see that this witness writes about the murder of Samir Trako, that he talks about all the figures relative to the on-site inspection, and that he points out that the scene of the crime had been tampered with, just as he told the Court yesterday. Furthermore, on page 5 of these notes, we can also see that on the 2nd of March, '93, Esad Salkic was killed, Miroslav Bralo is mentioned again, and again he speaks about the alleged brutality of the latter. On page 6, the murder of Bosnian officers and the conduct of the Military Police by the Vitez Hotel is also mentioned, and Vlado Santic's conduct. Lastly, on page 8 of these notes, we see the events on the 26th of March, '93, when the witness heard Vlado Santic's voice and, in particular, mentions Ivan Josipovic who told the witness, according to what he said yesterday, that Vlado Santic had been an active participant in the attack. Now, if we relate the answers of the witness to the Prosecutor's questions and when we look at these notes and we see that the Prosecutor examined the witness in the order and as to the substance of these notes, so I should first like to hear from the Prosecution, how could the Prosecution follow the exact order of this if, as the Prosecutor said yesterday, he knew nothing about this, if he did not have these notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like to reiterate that I did not have these notes. It is, however, an oversight and a regrettable oversight that these notes were not turned over to the Defence earlier, and it was an oversight in the sense that we simply did not notice in the original statement that the notes were attached, and for that we are sorry. I can certainly provide for the Court a brief history of how we came to speak to this witness and how it came about that these questions were asked, if the Court desires? This witness was interviewed in '98 by an investigator in Central Bosnia in connection with another investigation, and it was not an interview, it was just a discussion and not a signed interview, and during the course of that discussion, it became clear that this witness had some information about Mr. Santic. On the strength of those notes, we asked Mr. Zlotrg to come to The Hague to be proofed for possible testimony, and during the course of talking to him, he provided a lot of information, and we culled it down to the information that I felt was relevant to the Tribunal, those dates. Having now seen the translation of his notes, it certainly is clear to me that as he was talking to me, he was speaking from his knowledge of what happened during the incident, and his knowledge is based, to a large extent, on what he saw and what he observed, and also as it was recorded in his notes. And that's how I conducted the direct examination. The notes, I believe, should have been turned over. It was not. It is an oversight. But I did not have the notes. I did not have the English translation of the notes. I did not know what was in those notes. All I knew is what this witness was telling me during proofing, and what he was telling me during proofing is, as Defence counsel points out, consistent with, in fact, what he recollected in 1996 when he wrote the notes, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we again have not heard the answer as to how did he manage to observe the order in the substance of these notes, but I presume it is up to you, Your Lordships, to decide. The Prosecutor again affirms that he did not have these notes. Your Lordships, I should like to tell you, and of course you can either trust me or check it, that in the records of the Furundzija case, the Prosecutor's Office gave these notes to the Prosecution (sic) even in their English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In Furundzija? You say in Furundzija?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the Furundzija case. These notes were given to the Defence and including their English translation. I checked that, and you can also get the same information. Now, in this regard, I should like to address the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We believe that -- I don't doubt that what you just said is correct in the Furundzija case -- but you should take into account that in the Furundzija case, a different team from the Office of the Prosecutor took part in the proceedings, so the trial attorneys from the Prosecution were other persons, and probably there was a lack of contact between the various teams of the OTP. This is one point. My second point is that we don't question and we will not question the good faith and the professional attitude of Mr. Moskowitz. I am sure that this was an oversight. Third point: On the other hand, as soon as you realised that there were notes, they were passed on to you and you had the opportunity to go through the notes, and this morning you are going to cross-examine the witness on the basis of those notes. The final point, I would not overemphasise the importance of this problem because, in any case, these are peripheral matters. Let's be very clear about this. The matters raised in this testimony really are not of crucial importance. Therefore, as I say, I think we could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, I am happy to hear that that is how you see it. To my mind, this testimony is more important and it seems that I accord more attention to this problem than it really deserves on the face of it. I nevertheless have to say that we, on the Defence team, and regardless of what Mr. Moskowitz says, we are really quite worried about what happened, and I am not really convinced that this was merely an oversight. However, it is, as I have said, up to you to decide, and I won't dwell on that. The statement that was given to us, that is a statement in which there is not a word about the witness saying -- I mean, if you have to prepare for a cross-examination, you don't only read the notes. I could, of course, read those notes about a dozen times. But to my mind, preparing for cross-examination, it means to verify the claims, the affirmations, in a particular statement, and I think that the provisions of 66A of our Rules, which says that not less than -- will permit the Defence to inspect any documents and so on and so forth, and the purpose of this is to do it really in due time and to allow them to verify the information suggested. So the cross-examination cannot be based only on logical, semantic, linguistic, or any other verifications of the trustworthiness of a witness. The witness talks about facts that I have heard for the first time and which I could not verify. For instance, the witness asserted that Ivan Josipovic, the brother of the wife of the accused, told him that Vlado Santic had been an active participant in the attack. Now, this is a serious accusation even if hearsay. Yesterday, I talked to the wife of the accused, and she says, "my brother has excellent relations with me and with my husband. My brother was in a camp where he was badly beaten and barely saved his life in the camp of the B and H army," and that is where our witness could have contact with him. And, of course, if it is true what he says, it is under those circumstances, when his life was in danger, that he could have said that -- what the witness asserts that he said. So this is one of the things and there are very many other things for which I really think I am entitled to prepare for cross-examination very conscientiously, very carefully. But, as the Prosecutor acted in contravention of Rule 66A(i) and not under C, and I really think that he has denied the right of the Defence and, in a way, infringed upon the right of the Defence, so will you please decide whether I am entitled to time for preparation of the cross-examination as this material was disclosed to me only yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In light of the serious objections made by Defence counsel, since actually an oversight did occur on the part of the Prosecution, and also considering that the testimony does not appear to be of crucial importance, we have decided to disallow this testimony, and so therefore, we will not take into account in any way the testimony given by the present witness, as if it had never been given to the Court. So this for the sake of respecting the rights of the Defence. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It may be a bit late to offer an alternative solution, but one thing that occurred to me, because we do view this testimony as somewhat important and would hate to see that it not be considered by the Tribunal, as I understand it, we will begin, at the end of November, with the Defence case, and would request consideration to this possibility, that the witness be called back on that date or the day before or before the Defence case begins to be cross-examined by Defence counsel to the extent they need to cross-examine him. That will provide them with more than sufficient time to prepare for whatever cross-examination they feel that Defence counsel needs and it would also allow the evidence to be preserved so that the Tribunal can consider it at the end of the case. We do feel that some of this testimony is quite significant, and so we would request the Tribunal to consider that alternative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, actually, we had already considered the option you had just offered and had ruled it out, so therefore, we stick to our decision. As a result also, the document handed yesterday by the Prosecution, which is Exhibit 313, will not be taken into account. In any case, it was given only for identification purposes. It will not be taken into account. So I -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, Your Honour, on Exhibit 313. We did offer it only to -- for identification purposes with the hope of authenticating it in another manner at a later date, and because we received this document only at the end of our case, we would hope to be able to be allowed to find some way to authenticate it, either with another witness, although that appears to be unlikely, or through perhaps handwriting samples from Mr. Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No. We had already decided yesterday afternoon that we would not allow any such checking of the handwriting of the accused, and we had decided to ask Defence counsel whether they dispute the contents of the agreement, regardless of whether or not this agreement was signed by one of the accused, whether you agree that an agreement was made. If you were not to dispute that, we thought that we could take into account this agreement as signed by somebody called Zoran, without putting any family name next to the first name. Again, let me ask you whether you -- although at this stage this question has become somewhat moot -- however, since you may wish to introduce this document to -- this exhibit again, you said that you are going to see whether it can be authenticated, let me just explore and see what the position of the Defence counsel is. Counsel Radovic? About the contents of the agreement, the contents, without the question of who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We are contesting the authenticity of the document. We are contesting -- we dispute the possibility that Zoran Kupreskic might have signed such a document or taken part in such an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, I agree, I agree, because, as I say, we cannot verify and we will never allow the taking of any sample of the handwriting of the accused. The question is whether you also dispute the contents of the agreement, leaving aside the question of who signed it -- because we would never say in any case it was signed by one of the accused. Do you also contest that the agreement was signed, was made -- was made by the two parties concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We know nothing about that agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Then it cannot be taken into account, and we will now give back the document to the registrar. I will now turn to the witness to thank him. I think there is no objection to the witness being released now in light of the ruling just made, and so I will thank you for coming here to give evidence in court. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We should now come back to the other witness, Mr. Nihad Rehibic. Yes, Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Lordships. Mr. President, I have a question. On the 7th of October this year, Witness DD appeared before this Court. We have the statement of her previous interview with the Tribunal's investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: On the 5th and 15th of March. That is, after the indictment was filed and confirmed. Since the date on that statement is later than the date of the indictment, we think that this is a very important and serious case, and we are really, I think, entitled to assume that this witness had already given a statement to the Commission for War Crimes of the B and H, and we have some working notes submitted to us by the Prosecution of the 15th of July, '93, and refers to the conflict in Ahmici. Now, as that witness, in her testimony, says that four persons had been killed by her house and three houses and other buildings had been lit afire, I assume that she had already been examined by the Commission for the finding of facts on the perpetration of crimes in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I should like to ask the Court, in view of the evidence Rules -- or, rather, 74, to submit all of the statements which this witness had given to that Commission. I believe it would be in the interests of justice because the testimony, the statement of this witness, runs completely contrary to what other witnesses relative to other events said, and those were statements which were given during 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, as far as Witness DD is concerned, pursuant to an application under Rule 66, we submitted to the Defence all the statements we had, and indeed when this witness was heard, we produced not a statement but notes, rather, coming from an investigator, notes that were not signed. The Tribunal asked for an affidavit. This will be done tonight or tomorrow morning at the latest, but probably tonight. We transmitted all the elements we had at our disposal. If there were other hearings from other organisations, we have not been informed about these hearings, and the Defence which is asserting this has to verify this. I think that as far as this witness is concerned, we respected our obligations; therefore, I don't understand the request of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We think that the position of the Prosecution is the right one. If they did not know of any document or statement, they were not in a position to turn over those statements to the Defence, and it is for the Defence counsel to try to get hold of those statements, either directly or through the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is made difficult for us. I just asked the Court that this be prepared via the Court in the sense of Rule 74 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What do you mean? Rule 74 on amicus curiae?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I wanted to propose, Mr. President, that the Court should get from the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina statements by this witness, because the working notes say that she was questioned by the Commission for War Crimes of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so she was questioned concerning this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So this is not the relevant provision of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. So why don't you put in a request, a written request, and we will comply with it and we will forward your request to the authorities? If you wish, we will say we are asking the authorities to provide that document to the Court so that it can be used when it comes to the Defence case, it will be useful for your Defence when we open the Defence case in late November. We would also like to ask you, in your written request, to specify how many statements were given by that witness to the Bosnian authorities and, if possible, when, so that our request to the Bosnian authorities will be quite accurate and specific. If you have some details, I mean, any details would be useful to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We may now move on to our witness. Now, let me check. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac was to cross-examine the witness, and meanwhile, she has had an opportunity, I hope, to go through the hand-written list, HVO identification list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will try to compare the two lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yesterday we talked to the witness, Mr. Moskowitz and myself, related to the photocopying of these notes. We only thought that the witness should say before the Court, relating to the persons listed here as far as number 90 something. There are some notes next to these numbers. We want to ascertain who made these notes, these additional notes, and how they were made, who they were verified with. We want to hear this from the witness in order to avoid possible misunderstandings later on. We would like to hear that from him, how he made these notes, how he -- what he wrote in his own hand, and what was not the original list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Will you please answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yesterday I said on this day I was tasked by the commander, Mr. Sefkija, to conduct the action of the reception and burial of the bodies. The procedure was explained by me. After the burial, from the list I had received, I handed one copy to the Commission and one I kept. I wrote the ordinal numbers according to the list of the HVO. For non-identified persons, bodies, I didn't write anything, I just wrote the number. Where there was the first and last name, I only took this information from the HVO list. Later, for my own needs, I put some brackets and noted where the corpses, the bodies, might have come from. This was my personal view or finding. Later, more bodies were brought by UNPROFOR, and I made some notes, "charred body," et cetera. Two more bodies were brought which were numbered which I also wrote in my notes, and when I saw these numbers, I compared in my notes that on those numbers there already was some information, some description. Then I went to the inspector to compare the two lists, and then, in my list, when we did this comparison, on the left side I marked where it was identical, the notes were tallied and where they did not tally. Where they were not the same -- in one case I made an error, it seems to me. I didn't check carefully enough so ... There were some discrepancies under the same ordinal number, two persons, two bodies were brought. These were my private notes, notes for myself, and then I told Mr. Vatras that they should analyse in detail the lists and also enter it into the documentation so that the documents may be presented later on. On that day, only on that day, I was tasked to do that job because (redacted) wasn't able to do it. He would have been too shaken by this. The list that I showed the investigators I took from the command of the brigade and added -- enclosed to the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was the list that you received from the HVO, are these their ordinal numbers, their numbers? They didn't have more, several lists.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did say that there were two lists. One I gave to the criminal department and one I kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: They were copies, not two separate lists, and the numbers were the same as they are now in your lists?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In one of the lists, not in the second, not in the second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What is the second?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was given to the service, to the department which worked on the identification that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All that is in brackets or outside the brackets and identifies the places where the people were found, these are your assumptions?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, my personal assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Not confirmed. And you have no other data which would determine the site where the corpses were found?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I couldn't find that. I left Stari Vitez on April the 4th, and I didn't deal with the case -- with this any more. I didn't feel the need to add any information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All those parts, when you say Ahmici, Santici, and when there is no identification of the corpse, this is your own assumption?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is my personal observation, my personal note.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moskowitz? I assume -- all Defence counsel have duly cross-examined the witness, so we can see whether Mr. Moskowitz has any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes. Just a few questions, Your Honour, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Rehibic, that the day of the burial was a very difficult day for you and other people there?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely. Never in my life have I felt worse that on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And it was a very difficult assignment to try to bury a hundred people in a couple of hours and establish some sort of identity for those people?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly. We deviated from the plan, the previous plan. We had planned to individually examine every body to compare it to the list, to the records that were given us, but we were short of time so that the burial did not follow our original plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So you, I take it, did the best job you could, to try to make the best identification you could of a hundred bodies in a couple of hours?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And you relied on the identifications provided to you by the HVO for the most part?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For the most part, we did use their documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Your notes here, as you fully admit, contain some mistakes, but they were done quickly and they were done as accurately as you could?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These notes are identical as concerns the numbers, and the unknown persons, unknown bodies, were in the list; there was an unidentified person, body, I wrote the name. The other notes I made later without any purpose, without intending to use it for any definite purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you have those notes with you that you could look at right now?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Here are the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, looking at Sukrija Ahmic, which is listed as number 6 in the list that your people did, and it says, "Brought in as number 90," according to the HVO list, could you look at your notes and see what you have for number 90?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Under number 90, I have Ahmic Sukrija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And that identification would come from the HVO? They identified this man as Sukrija Ahmic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And then under the typed list is Meho Hrustanovic who was brought in as number 91. Who do you have for number 91 on the HVO list?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Also Meho Hrustanovic. I have him also under 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And again, that was a person identified by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And the HVO, as far as you knew, they were the ones that picked up these bodies?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the bodies were on the territory controlled by the HVO and they collected the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Then Aziz Pezer is listed as number 95 on the HVO list. What do you have in your notes for 95?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Number 95 is Pezer Aziz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And then Sabahudin Zec is listed as number 96 on the HVO list. What do you have in your notes for number 96?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my notes too, number 96 is Zec Sabahudin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Number 53 on the HVO list is listed as an unknown male. What do you have for number 53 on your HVO list?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Number 53 I have nothing. This was unknown, NN. In such cases, I didn't write in anything. I just wrote the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And with regard to those that were unknown, were there further attempts after the burial and after this list was compiled, to try to identify, as best you could, those unknown people?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Later, when we finished the burial, I didn't take an active part in the identification. When I left the town, when I went to my family, who were refugees, displaced persons, in talking to people I heard that under 68, Ibrahim Karic was alive. I crossed him out without further verification. This was my personal note. I didn't feel the need to inquire further because there was a service, a special service, for that. I also heard about another person who was still alive and who was listed as dead and I also wrote it in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And these mistakes of listing people who were dead that were, in fact, still alive, those were mistakes on the HVO list; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So the HVO made mistakes too, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These are the identical data from the HVO list that I received on the day of the burial. Without these additional notes, subsequent notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Just a couple more. Fahrudin Ahmic, son of Hasim, is listed as number 57 in the HVO list, in the list that your team drafted. What do you have in your notes for number 57?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I also have Ahmic Fahrudin listed as 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, look at number 38 and see if there is a mistake there. Not number 38 in your list, but look at Abdulah Brko, brought in as number 23 from the HVO list -- that is the information we have on the typed list that was submitted by your team that this Abdulah Brko was brought in as number 23. Who do you have as number 23 on the HVO list?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the number where under the same number two bodies were brought, Redzib Halib is on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Is that possibly an error or is there an explanation you can provide for why, on the typed list, Brko Abdulah is listed as number 23 on the HVO list whereas on your notes 23 is a different person, Halib Redzib?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is probably an error in the list we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes. And if you look at the typed list, Halib Redzib is the next person listed and he also, that body also is said to have been brought in as number 23 on the HVO list. So it appears that there bodies were brought under the same number 23 from the HVO list. Apparently some error was made either with the HVO list or with your list.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Our list couldn't contain errors because when we received the bodies and when we buried them, we marked with numbers the buried bodies according to the HVO list, which was in the possession of the inspector. The list I had was of this content, and the inspector's notes are the same as those of the army of the criminal police, of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a little while ago Ibrahim Karic who was brought in or apparently brought in by the HVO and listed as number 68 on the HVO list, number 51 on the typed list. What do you have if your notes for Ibrahim Karic? What number was he on the HVO list?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On this list, Ibrahim Karic was 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: But that was a mistake because he, in fact, was not dead?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't confirm, I can't say "Yes" or "No." When I left Stari Vitez, I heard from people that he is alive, but I didn't check it. I didn't pursue the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: No more questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have only a couple of questions, minor questions, on your notebook. On pages 12 and 13, if you could pick up your notebook? I see that there is a different handwriting from the one on the previous pages. Could you tell me whose handwriting this was?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Even on page 12 and 13?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And then on each page, I saw that some numbers have been ticked off by you, say on page 7, numbers 18, 19, 20. Then the next page, number 22 and 23. And then page 9, almost all of these numbers. What does this ticking off mean?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Today I already said that on the day of the burial, 94 bodies were buried. UNPROFOR brought more bodies to the cemetery, to the burial ground. When two bodies were brought which were marked as 70 and 69, then in my notes I looked at numbers 69 and 70 to see what was there. At 69, I had Pjanic Muhamed and 70 was Ahmic Munib. The bodies were brought by UNPROFOR without any data, without any data. This prompted me to ask the inspector to compare the two lists we had on the first day of the burial. We started this comparison. And on my list, I ticked off those numbers where the data were identical in the two lists, the inspector's list and the one that I kept for myself and from which I made my notes. Where they were identical, I put these ticks, I ticked them off, and when I -- when they were not identical, I stopped doing it, and the inspector continued with the comparison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. I think there is no objection to the witness being released. Mr. Rehibic, thank you for giving evidence. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. We will break now for coffee until twenty-five past eleven, and the next witness will be Mr. Kujawinski?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It will be Witness No. 8 on the list, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We need a number for the notes. These, I assume, have been admitted into evidence. I don't remember whether we decided anything on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We will formally offer it into evidence at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So it is Prosecution Exhibit ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number 314.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So these are the notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I am afraid we will break now, and, I'm sorry, you will come back in 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you tell the Court what is your name and your position at the moment?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Howard Tucker. I'm a British police officer on secondment to the Criminal Tribunal. I'm employed as an investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor. My experience is I'm a police officer, 27 years' experience, 23 years as a detective officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, recently you executed a mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and to be more precise, in Ahmici; is that true?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: One of the tasks you were assigned was to measure some distances in Ahmici, and I will ask the usher to submit two documents to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map is Exhibit 315 and the list is 316.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, on the first document, Exhibit 315, we can see an aerial photograph of Ahmici, and on this photograph, in metres, we can see a certain number of distances.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you do these measurements yourself, and if so, how did you proceed?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I took the measurements myself, Your Honours, and it was a combination of two methods: one was by use of a motor vehicle and the use of the tropometer of that vehicle, and of other method was to pace some of the distances myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The second document, Exhibit 316, is the summary of all the distances that were indicated on the aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I will ask Mr. Usher to submit three photographs to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits 317, 318, and 319.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, another task that was assigned to you was to look for and photograph a place where vegetables and fruits were stored. This place had been mentioned by a witness during these proceedings. And this has to do with the death of Fata Pezer. Did you manage to find this place and where did you find it?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. After a short search of the area, in front of the house that I know as House B, I found this actual structure. The distance is approximately 30 metres from the front of House B, below the ground level, in an area that is surrounded by vegetation and a small fruit orchard, and it was actually well-hidden from view at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What does the photograph which has been put on the ELMO represent?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: That is the actual entrance to the structure I'd describe as being a fruit store. It was hidden by undergrowth, natural undergrowth. Not hidden as such, but not visible because of natural undergrowth. The door to the structure is actually open and that is actually how it was when I came across it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can photograph 318 be put on the ELMO, please? What does this photograph depict and where was it taken from?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I was actually standing in front of the structure I've just described, Your Honours. The structure is to my left, and I'm actually facing a house which is -- which I've identified as House 51 from the map that I understand Your Honours have seen. It is facing the general direction of the lower mosque of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next photograph, please? What does this photograph depict and where did you take it from?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm still standing at this position in front of the structure. I'm standing with my right-hand side to the entranceway, I'm looking in the general direction of Upper Ahmici at this point, directly the opposite way to the last photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The place of which the photograph you've taken, is it the place that existed before, that is, on April the 16th, 1993, or were there some changes in the landscape?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: The landscape, as I understand it, has changed quite considerably from as it was in 1993, and in this particular photograph, you can see evidence of the changes. The ground that you see directly in front of you where that tree is has been earth movements, it has been back-filled, is the best way I can describe it, into the area immediately in front of this structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How far, approximately, was the door of the fruit store from the House number 51, the house we saw on picture 318, the previous photograph, I mean? How far was it?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I would estimate that that's about 35 to 40 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, can we have the big photograph, the big aerial photograph, which is behind you, and could you submit this photograph to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, using the pointer, could you show approximately, since we don't have a very precise map, where the entrance to the fruit store is on this aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It's approximately in that spot here, at the base of the hill, House B, just about that area (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now ask Mr. Usher to show you seven photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits 320 to 326.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please review briefly the seven photographs and make the remarks that you deem necessary, but first of all, we would like to know where these photographs were taken, where from, and what they depict generally, and maybe you could show, using the aerial photograph, the places where the pictures were taken from?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was asked to try to locate a position that was known as a bridge or something similar near to the junction of Ahmici which had a gully or something similar running underneath it. The location was pointed out to me before I went away to Bosnia, so I knew roughly the location of the gully, and this is the location of that particular item. It's about 200 metres east of the junction with Ahmici. The position roughly -- the exact position on the map, overhead map, is this point here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: My apologies. The gully runs in this direction and passes under the road at this point and continues in the direction as depicted on the map. The first photograph, which is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we cannot see anything that the witness is showing. I mean, the way he's sitting, we simply cannot see a thing on this photograph, or what he is pointing to. So whether we may stand up or something, we simply cannot see this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you move the photograph? Is that better?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: To start again, Your Honours -- is that better?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: This is the gully I was referring to to Their Honours. It passes under the road at this point and then continues its journey, as you can see from the aerial map. The distance I estimate from here to the junction of Ahmici is about 200 metres, and the first photograph is taken looking in the general direction of this structure here (indicating), taken from this point, and showing the south side of the gully itself. And from the photograph, the gully passes under the road at this point adjacent to that blue vehicle. The second photograph is taken from the same spot but actually facing the south side of the road to show the point where the gully passes under the road, and you can see as a point of reference this item here is a crash barrier which is actually -- it's broken and laying on the roadside, but at that point that is where the gully exits on the south side of the road. The next photograph, I'm actually standing alongside the structure which is the broken crash barrier and looking into the gully itself. At this point here is where it exits from underneath the roadway and continues its journey. And the following photograph is seen from a similar position but actually showing the route of what is or was at this time a very small stream or brook at the base of the gully with a small amount of water running through it. This photograph is taken on the opposite side of the road to the last one, so I'm back onto the north side of the road looking into the gully, the direct opposite of the photograph I showed just now, and this is generally the gully itself actually going back upwards in the general direction of the village of Ahmici, and it just shows the vegetation and the general route of the gully itself. And then the last two photographs -- I'll show them separately first but then they can be overlaid to give a general idea of the terrain itself -- this is again from the south side of the road (indicating). That's the fallen crash barrier and the actual brook, stream exits under the road at about this point here and continues its journey. And that's just a continuation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking you to slow down a little bit, if you can, please?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. And this final photograph is a continuation of the previous, and it can be overlaid at a point like that to roughly show the route of the ravine and -- I beg your pardon -- the gully and the stream as it leaves the underside of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to remind the Court that this place has something to do with the statement of Abdulah Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What was the height between the bottom of the gully and the road itself?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Approximately 4 metres to the base where the stream was, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like now Prosecution Exhibit 208 to be submitted to the witness, and I would like you to mark on this exhibit -- this is an aerial photograph, Ahmici aerial photograph -- to mark the two sites that you took pictures of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Maybe you could put it on the desk because the witness is going to mark it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I will now ask you to mark where the fruit store was that you indicated before with an arrow and with letter "A" please, as precisely as you can, of course.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And then could you please mark the gully where it goes under the road with an arrow and with letter "B"?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have this document put on the easel so the Defence counsel can see the marks put by the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We can't see the marks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Point "A" (indicating) and Point "B" showing the route of the gully under the road (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. Another of your tasks was to look in Bosnia, and particularly in Zenica, to look for the original of a video cassette of a witness. This witness was questioned at the hospital when he was getting treatment for burns on his hands. Can you tell us if you managed to locate the original of this video cassette?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Your Honours, not during my time in Bosnia, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We are, let us say, satisfied with the answer to the question as to whether the original of the tape will be obtained, but we should like to present our attitude as regards that tape, if you like. So we shall admit -- we shall recognise that Sakib Ahmic gave an interview, what we have been told was a part of his interview, but we are affirming that it is not the whole of the interview, I mean the part that we saw on the tape that was shown us is not the whole of the interview which Sakib Ahmic gave. I'm sorry for this interruption, but we simply thought we should mention it now when we come to the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Will you be in a position, Counsel Radovic, to get hold of the original of this document, of the videotape? Do you think you may? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately -- I mean, we tried to get something, anything, regarding the subject, and without success. But we are happy that the Prosecution can provide us with at least a part of this videotape so that we know that it is in existence, as we were trying to do it through witnesses who had seen the programme. Now we shall use the witnesses to refer to the rest of the tape which has not been shown to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am not sure I quite understood what Counsel Radovic said. I would like to underline the fact that Counsel Radovic is now saying that the witness we are talking about was questioned longer than what is shown on the video that was presented to the Court. We don't have any evidence of this. This is an assertion made by Counsel Radovic to this Chamber. Maybe he can prove this. But at this stage, today, it's only an assertion by Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like to ask some clarification to the witness. Even though he didn't locate the original, which would be a video except longer than the one we obtained through the witness, he managed nevertheless to find a videotape which has a number of complimentary elements, so could you please tell us what you found there?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Your Honours, as a result of the inquiries I started in Bosnia, the result was that a tape is being presented through the internal workings in Bosnia and has arrived here. It's an almost identical duplicate of the one the Court has already seen, but it actually shows a short conversation -- introduced a short conversation introduced by the interviewer of the witness. Unfortunately, we don't know the identity yet of that interviewer, but what that interviewer has said has been translated, and I think Mr. Prosecutor has a copy of that translation and the original Bosnian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to hand to this Chamber and to Defence counsel, first of all, the videotape the witness has just talked about, a transcript of the several sentences that were not in the first videotape and that you will hear at the beginning of the videotape, and finally, minutes, so to speak, which were given to the Prosecutor of this videotape which was signed not only by the Prosecutor which received the document but also by Saharik Assan (phoen), President of the Investigative Commission on War Crimes and a Minister of the Interior in Zenica. So there are three documents, the cassette, the transcript, and the minutes, which I shall now hand to the Chamber through this testimony. We indicated that there may be an original, that this original may be constituted of other declarations; however, we did not manage to locate so far this video, if it exists. But, of course, we asked our investigators to go on looking for this document in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have more details on where this cassette comes from? Who filmed the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In fact, we don't know precisely which organisation, official or other, filmed this interview, why, and we don't know either if this film was broadcast and when. But I may ask the question to the witness ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, did you obtain information about the person or the organisation which filmed the interview of the witness and for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Your Honours, unfortunately, it was not possible to find out who or why the film was taken. There are two possibilities if it was an officially televised programme. One is by a local Central Bosnian television organisation, and there's a suggestion that it may well have been an outside Croatian broadcast as well, and this has been part of the difficulty in trying to establish exactly who, why, and when the film footage was taken. The search is still continuing and we are still hopeful that we will be able to resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, for clarification, is this tape you referred to Exhibit 157, at least the transcript is 157, I think? Could we be told what this is an addition to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. However, the tape we are now giving to the Court is the same videotape with a comment which was not on the first exhibit, that is, on Exhibit 157, but the witness is saying the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think this cassette was shown already because one of the witnesses told us that he was told that we had seen the videotape and that Sakib Ahmic had been seen on the film, so maybe it was broadcast on the local TV channel. So I'm wondering if it's really necessary to express an official request. Maybe the Tribunal could ask the Bosnian authorities to provide the original of this tape or a copy of the whole video cassette.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I interrupt one second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The request you have just made I have already made to the Bosnian authorities and that is actually in hand at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video is Exhibit 327, the transcript is 327A, and the minutes are 327B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Judge May has a good point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suggest it be added to 157 in some way so that it is all part of the same exhibit. 157B or ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Then the whole set will be 157A? Is that okay? 157A for the video, the transcript, and the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you are finished, Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, do you want to speak to one of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I understand what they want. They want -- they don't want something to be entered into evidence that they didn't see. They don't know what the cassette contains. They haven't seen it. They are just checking what it is, and that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You're right. Let us show, yes, the video cassette. Yes. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I can say before we see the video cassette, we see from the text that we have been given by the Prosecution, we see the content of the introductory part. We now say that we don't have the whole cassette because the final part is missing. What we have been given shows us that the first cassette was not complete, not the complete interview. It was cut to suit the needs of the person who had it. The introductory part shows us that the whole video cassette was not submitted, but we are interested in the final part, which we don't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to repeat it once more. It has not been proven that there is another part to this video cassette. That is what Counsel Radovic says. But it has not been proven so far, and we didn't find any elements that tend to prove it. Of course, if the Chamber wants to show the video so that Defence counsel know exactly what we have tendered -- but there is a transcript of the introduction of the sequence that was not on the original Exhibit 157. But if they want to see the videotape, I think it would be possible, it's just two minutes, two and a half minutes, so that could be a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I said that the final part was missing not off the cuff because when we were looking for our Defence witnesses, we knew of the existence of the programme, and we were looking for people who saw it because we didn't know whether we would get the tape, and the evidence of our witnesses -- we have found three or four such persons who came from Zenica to Vitez -- they will tell us what the end of the tape contained. So I'm not saying something that I haven't thought about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Let us now show the videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't really understand. Which is the part of the video that was not included in the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It's the very brief comment at the very beginning of the videotape, but we don't see the author of this comment, and this is the transcript that we obtained from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic, who is going to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness will be cross-examined by Ranko Radovic, Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac, and Borislav Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I will be very brief and I will put just a few technical questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, when you went to Vitez, you had the task of measuring certain distances, if I understood your task, the purpose of your going to Vitez, that is, to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: That was part of it, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In order to do this task, what technical equipment were you carrying?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I had no technical equipment, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because I am surprised. In your report you say that you carried out the measurement with your -- with your -- walking or with a device that is on the car, a distance measurer. What do surveyors use?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: There is a metal meter which is dragged on the ground in order to obtain the precise measurements. Do you know what is used in traffic accidents to measure distances?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I know what's used in traffic accidents, sir, but the object of this exercise was for an approximate distance, not a precise distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to the scene, why was it problematic to take precise measurements? because for some matters this may be of great importance, a difference of 50 metres may play a great role. Explain, please, why you went to do this measurement without any equipment.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: It wasn't my task. My task was to take approximate measurements, sir, which is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Approximate measurements. All right. I'm satisfied with your answer, but I'm not satisfied with a situation in which a person travels to carry out measurements, there is equipment, and that person doesn't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, there is no English translation. MR. TERRIER (in English): I just wanted to say that the distances on the map are not proven to be wrong at this time, so there is no argument possible now from Mr. Radovic. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, but Mr. Radovic is arguing - and I think that this is a good point - that these are not accurate distances. The measurements were not accurate, were approximate. And his point is, why did the investigator go there just to give us approximate measurements?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Approximate, not exact. We are not in a technical situation; it is not an air crash or a traffic accident where we are concerned about centimetres and inches. It was not the right attitude but we thought that it was the procedure we had to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about distances, I am not talking about centimetres, I am talking about metres, dozens of metres. If you make such a long trip, go on such a long trip, then it's worth doing it properly. All witnesses talked about approximate distances. We didn't need an expert to ascertain approximate distances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let us now leave aside any methodological dispute. You may question the method, but what matters is whether or not the distances are accurate. If you dispute anything, we can check with modern technical equipment. My colleagues are suggesting that you can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Even with old-fashioned devices, the iron meter that you used to drag on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Counsel Radovic. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tucker. It seems to me that there are other errors here. It is not only a matter of distance. The instructions you were given are not too precise. Point 4, item 4, point 4, you do have the map in front of you? Point 4. Point 4. What is marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Point 4 at this location.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what, according to you, is it?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: That's the location of a structure called the Sutre warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Sutre warehouse is on another -- in another part. This is a company called Ogrjev Fuel. This is quite a different site. The measurements were done in relation to this spot, in relation to several locations, from the crossroads towards Ahmici, Sutre warehouse, towards Santici on several occasions, and it is obvious that the site it wrong, that this is wrong. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: If you say that's an oil -- an oil warehouse did you say, Ma'am? An oil warehouse? Then I won't dispute that. [The following passage is mixed interpretation, i.e. two interpreters speaking intermittently]

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't understand. This point marked 4 exists on the ground. It was measured in relation to other points ... what it represents, but it doesn't really matter. It's just the fact that he put on the map measurements that he took on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I don't understand. It is not clear to me. Sutre warehouse is number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, there was a mistake. There is really a mistake. What counts is the distance from number 4 to number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is precisely where the Sutre warehouse is. It is on that parking lot from the Sutre warehouse which is located on that white area to Ahmici, to the road, and the road to Ahmici, the distance is more than 400 metres if the gentleman measured from the point on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: The points that I have measured are from 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 4, 4 to 5, and 5 to 6, irrespective of what the locations are called, Ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Did you measure from 3 to 10, because Sutre warehouse is at number 10?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. From 3 to 7, from 7 to 16? Did you measure this -- 300 metres are from number 7 to number 16?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes, 7 to 16. The measurements then run from point 3 to point 7, point 7 to point 8, 8 to 9, and then we have 7 to 16, and then we have 10 to 11, 11 to 12, 12 to 13, 10 to 14, 14 to 15, and 15 to 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That's walking along the road or along the paths. That's how you did it?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: In which part, Ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Everywhere. You are going from number to number. You are walking on the road or roads or the paths.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Either walking or in a vehicle, Ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. I'm interested in the following -- these distances are very important for us. They are essential. You said the distance from number 5, the crossroads towards Santici --

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: -- to the Sutre warehouse, which is at number 4, this is 400 metres --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Will you please listen? The point is that there is a mistake about the Sutre warehouse. It is not the Sutre warehouse, it is point 4. The way to look at this is simply to look at the numbers and not be concerned with the description on Exhibit 315.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. That's what I wanted to say in one part, and in the other part I wanted to say ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How do we get distances by adding them up? How do we get -- and that's why I asked whether these measurements are made by using the roads and the paths. Were the movements along the road or along the path? That's what I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Generally or in any particular point?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to points 16 to 15.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: That last stretch from 15 to 16 is an approximation, and the reason for that was there was a heavily overgrown in the areas of the footpath, and that is an approximation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And 15 to 14 also, where there are no paths, I suppose, I expect that you had to approximate, you had to determine the distances approximately.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. The point 14 to 15 is an approximation. Point 10 to 14 is paced out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: One more thing. This also belongs to methodology. What did the Prosecutor mean when he marked certain positions? Under "M," you have House B. This has to be checked on the large map, up to point 14. Which object was marked as point 14? We don't know what distance the Prosecution was determining there.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: The point of reference was left really to me when I went up there to see exactly what the lay of the land was. That point of reference, 10 to 14, point 14 represents something I can really describe as a rough footpath and where the footpath naturally bends. It seemed to be the easiest point of reference to be able to refer to the overhead map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: This means that number 14 is that bend on the path, on the footpath?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What about point 15?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Point 15 is a similar situation where the bend in the path, it doubles back down towards number 16, and there's another footpath that abuts it at that point, at number 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Point 16 was -- what was there? Was there the end of something? Was there a house, a facility, a warehouse, a parking lot, since it is not marked precisely and there are several objects or facilities there?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: At the corner of that particular warehouse, where the red number 1 is, virtually at the top of that 1, at that number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That is the corner of the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, you were measuring from the point -- the end of the arrow, not according to numbers but according to the arrows?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: The arrow shows the direction of the route taken or the anticipated route. It doesn't actually point to the end of the route itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We don't know it then. Tell us, number 1, point 1, where did you start from? Is it a bungalow, or is this the end of the map?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: The structure at number 1 is an actual lay-by in front of what I understand used to be the building known as the Bungalow, and that point actually started from the end of that lay-by, which is approximately where the arrow is there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: This point is on the map, where the structure was earlier, the house, or is it outside the map, because you used the map you were given?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, the map that I had was a larger-scale map to this, but, yes, where the number 1 is, that is at the location where the structure of the Bungalow was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are satisfied with ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Your Lordship, my colleagues have gone into this in considerable detail, but I shall be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell us if you have any surveying training. What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I am a police officer by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Have you been trained in land surveying? Are you an expert in these matters?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I have no training in land surveying at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have another question. You said you measured and on the photograph you show altitude distances around the gully. I think you were talking about these. So how did you calculate or how did you estimate the altitude differences?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Just by my observation, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Naked eye. By observation. You didn't use any aids or anything?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: No, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Just one more question. Here you made a photograph of that fruit store, I believe it is Exhibit 317, and did you do any measurements around that fruit store?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I did no measurements around the fruit store itself, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: So you wouldn't know its size or anything; you didn't go into it?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: No, I didn't go into it, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. I have no further questions. I should merely like to add that when we begin adducing our evidence, we shall bring in a professional, an expert, and we shall do it whenever this is of relevance for the Defence of our client, Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic, together with maps, surveying data, and all that. It will all be done very professionally. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no further questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I assume there is no objection to the witness being released? Mr. Tucker, thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until 2.00, and I hope at 2.00 we can quickly examine and cross-examine your last witness and then maybe move on to the Status Conference so that we can dispose of the Status Conference this afternoon. Again, let me repeat, if you have any questions or suggestions about the on-site visit, tell us this afternoon. So we will adjourn now until 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.38 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I wish to apologise for the delay, short delay. We had a meeting. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Lordship. Perhaps this is the right time, before the witness is brought in, to hear from the Prosecution about the evidence we tendered. I am referring to the certificate about the telephone call, the translation of all this, and then you said that the Prosecution -- I will say whether they object to it after they saw the text both in the Bosnian language and the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, was D5/6. We had the -- we were provided with the English text, and Counsel Pavkovic is right in asking whether the Prosecution has had the opportunity to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
