utterances.text: So it is admitted, both the English and the original Croatian version. Since we are talking of evidence, Exhibits -- the registrar kindly drew our attention to the need to formally admit into evidence the various statements made by the witness -- Witness SA, and you will be given copies, I understand, at the coffee break, and it will be Court Exhibit C1 through C6, six statements. So we have just been given copies, and you will receive copies at the coffee break. Okay. So we can move on to re-examination of the witness, Mr. Tucker. Do you have other questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No, no, no. We're finished with Mr. Tucker. This is another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. I'm a bit tired. I'm sorry. So we are going to hear the other witness, Mr. Kujawinski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Will you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will do so faithfully, independently, impartially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That is a pledge I think for Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon. Before we start, I would like you to tell the Judges what your name and your age is?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: My name is Andre Kujawinski, and I am 33 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You are a member of the British army. Can you tell us more precisely what are your current activities?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: At present, I am a CQMS, which is in charge of logistics within a company which is 120 in strength, within my unit, which is the 22nd Cheshire regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Judges your professional career and your military experience?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I've been in the army 15 years, taking one year's basic training, moving from there to Northern Ireland for a six-month tour, then moving out to Hong Kong for a two-year tour to visit places like Brunei, to do exercises. I was then promoted to a lance corporal at the end of the Hong Kong tour. Then we moved to Caetrim to undertake public duties of guarding the Queen. Whilst there, doing career courses and was promoted to Corporal. I then went to the depot to train and instruct recruits to join the army for a two-year tour. Whilst I was there, I did my next career courses to become a sergeant. Returned to my unit. They were in Chester. And then I was promoted to a sergeant as we went to Germany, to Fallingbastel, where I commanded then a platoon of 30 or so in strength. Whilst in Germany, we were posted to a six-month tour to Bosnia. After that tour and after Germany, I was then posted, again as a sergeant, to a careers office to recruit people into the army, for the regiment and for the army as a whole. I then came back to the unit again. Whilst in Oakington, where I was selected within the battalion and the division, which is seven regiments in all, to go and train officers at Sandhurst. I then went on that selection and successfully passed it. I stayed there for a tour of two years training officers for more countries for two years. I finished that in April just gone. I am now back with my unit. We have just moved from Northern Ireland to Chepstow, in South Wales where I have now been promoted again to a colour sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now going to talk about your tour in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Something was wrong with the interpretation regarding the military career of our witness. Speaking about his present post, he said he was doing something where there were seven divisions, and it can't be because a division is very large and therefore there can't be seven divisions in a battalion. They said he was with a battalion that had seven divisions and that is impossible so could we have it clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could the witness please clarify this question of divisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. I'm in a regiment, which is a member of a division which has seven units, which have seven regiments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It was a question of translation. Thank you. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let's now focus on your tour in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could you tell us when you were stationed in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I was stationed in the Vitez area from the November of '92 to the May, I think it was, May-April of '93 -- '93 to '94, sorry. And from the Vitez area we worked -- we went directly to Vitez from Germany. We then moved for a short period up to Tuzla, stopping at Kladanj, I think that's how you pronounce it, to setting up a forward operating base in Tuzla, in the airport. We then moved back to Vitez area to finish off the tour there. We did six months the whole tour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask you to clarify one point? You said that you were there in Vitez from November '92 to May-April '94?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, just a six-month tour. '92, sorry, to '93.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So May-April '93 then?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: During this time, what were your missions?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: We only had one mission and that was to get food and escort convoys to people who were directed from our Ops room, from our operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At the time, who was your command or, rather, what were your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I was a platoon sergeant in charge of a platoon of 30 or so men which entailed four Warrior armoured fighting vehicles. But towards the end of the tour, I was given a fifth vehicle which was my Battalion 2 IC's vehicle, as he came over and was not Warrior trained. And therefore his vehicle was not being used so he gave it to ourselves to be used and to be looked after, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let's now focus on the day of the 16th of April, 1993. I want to ask you to recall the morning you spent in Vitez, but rather the afternoon of the 16th. It seems that during that afternoon, you were called to Ahmici. First of all, I would like you to tell the Judges what were the reasons you were sent to Ahmici this day, the 16th of April, 1993, in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I was tasked from my Ops room to go to Ahmici to recover or help the aid of recovery of a vehicle from 9th-12th Lancers, a Scimitar, which is a smaller Warrior. They had a radio message to say one of their two vehicles had broken down in the village. I wasn't told it was Ahmici, I was just given a grid reference to go to. My vehicle, which was 22 bravo call sign, along with a REME vehicle which is a recovery vehicle which is also a Warrior but has no weapons on it, we immediately went off to Ahmici to find this vehicle which had been broken down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What time was it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: It was early afternoon, about 14.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How many vehicles were you responsible for during this mission?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: On this first visit, just the two vehicles, myself in a Warrior, and the vehicle behind which was the REME vehicle, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you now tell the Judges what you saw when you got closer to Ahmici, when you went through the village and when you entered the village, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. As I -- as we drove down the road towards the grid reference, again it wasn't Ahmici, I didn't know I was going to Ahmici at first, I was driving down the road, and we came to a prominent turn-off which was -- we called it the back road to Zenica, which is a mountain road which turned off to the left. There's always a roadblock there. There wasn't one this day. As we drove past slightly downhill we could see off to the left smoke billowing out beyond the skyline in several trickles of smoke. It wasn't just one complete trickle. We saw this, my driver and myself and the gunner that sits next to me, and at that point then we raced on because this stretch of road, from that Zenica turn-off down to the base of the road, I guess is about -- or was about a kilometre long, and we used to go fast down there just to give the vehicles a good run out, but this was more a case of getting there fast. We weren't used to seeing smoke at this stage in our tour. It wasn't a thing. So we raced down towards this road, slowed down, negotiated the turn which is to the left and to the right, and as we came up the hill mainly to the left we saw lots of houses destroyed, on fire, smoke billowing out, and people to the left of the road, people -- I say children and women, to the left of the road were lying in the open, appeared to me to be dead. We carried on driving down the road very slowly now. At this point I had forgot about my mission, which was to go to this grid to recover this vehicle because, quite obviously, other things had come to my mind. We drove very, very slowly down the road looking both left and right. To the right of the road wasn't much destruction. There's a couple of ruined houses, but nothing compared to as the left-hand side which is amazing, to say the least. We carried on driving down the road, again very slow. As we came to negotiate a left turn just past the cemetery which is on the right-hand side of the road, a woman jumped out from under the undergrowth with her arms -- with her hands clasped in a praying manner, and I couldn't understand what she was saying but her looks and her face was enough to tell me that she was very frightened and it was inevitable anyway that something was wrong. When I looked behind that, there was another three women and it looked to be a child behind her. We were stopped, it was slightly downhill. I told one of the soldiers from the back to go out and to go look at this woman, and I told him or told her through the soldier to wait there and we'll be back in ten minutes. He told her to go back into the undergrowth. She got back in -- it was like a mud bank, a large mud bank. She got back in and he then put some branches around her which were lying in the area and left them there. We then continued down the road. Now we switched back to what we were supposed to be doing, looking for the grid reference, and I drove off, again negotiating the bend very slowly to look to my left, to what we called the Swiss chalet which is a large tent-like building, a large triangular building with a large patio in the front area. Drove past that. Saw lots of people there. Negotiated a turn-around point, again a common point we used to call the turn-around point, it is where the road meets the river on a sharp bend. We turned around. As we turned round, we're now looking at the Swiss chalet to see there lots of soldiers. To date, of that time in Bosnia, that was the most amount of soldiers that I had saw, and I would call it a company group which to English military terms is a hundred or so soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a second. Could you give us some clarifications? You had with you a camera; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I carried a camera everywhere I went. Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And when you drove through Ahmici, you took a number of photographs; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct, sir. On both occasions that visit, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like the usher to show Exhibit number 53 to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this photograph depicts, or do you remember by seeing this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: The photograph was taken by myself on the first visit, the visit I'm talking about, and this here (indicating) is one of the viewing windows from the turret of the vehicle and it's the left-hand side of the road. We were driving in the direction I'm pointing. And it shows the burnt-out houses, bodies here and here, and houses on fire in the general area, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On the aerial photograph which is behind you, could you show us the places where you saw corpses or bodies?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Sir, the main road we drove down is the road here (indicating) and we saw bodies mainly on the left-hand side of the road, in this area here (indicating) and here, sir (indicating), and also this house here stands out because on the first drive again, as we drove down the area here being where we met the people huddled behind the mud bank, on the doorstep of this house there was what appeared to be a man which we thought was a father and his son lying in a not-so-comfortable way with lots of blood from the father's head, and there was a dog on the scene which was licking the blood off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Was this man alone?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, sir. He had a very young child with him, which we presumed was father and son lying down on the front doorstep of the house, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Just for reference, the house that has been shown by the witness on the aerial photograph is House number 49. If we refer to the other document, two people were dead in this house but not a father and son, as the witness has just said, it was a man, Mr. Pirjanovic born in 1950 and his wife born in 1958. Which means that today we cannot give any information about the precise identity of the two people saw by the witness in that particular place, and I have to remind you that a very high number of refugees were living in Ahmici at that period of time and that none -- not all of them were identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, let's go back to the Swiss cottage which you described. You said that there were a very significant number of soldiers in this Swiss cottage or outside. Could you describe the uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I was very close to them to start off with, sir, about no more than 30 yards at this point when we drove right up to them. The uniforms they were wearing were very dark. We were used -- at this point again to not seeing so many soldiers, as I've previously mentioned, but we weren't used to seeing so many military-styled-clothed people, it was just mixed dress, as we'd call it, which would be either civilian bottoms and a military top or the other way around. But this organised group was all wearing dark uniforms. I won't say it was black, I wouldn't say it was very dark green, it was just very dark uniforms, everyone of them was dressed like it. I also in my head saw -- and I've still got the memory now of a patch on one of the right arms. I've been through many files to try to identify the patch but I can't identify it. It was a shield. It was, as I'm looking at it from left to right, a stripe, a vertical stripe, a red, white, and blue, and there's an arched insignia across the top of it, but what it says, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, sir, lots of weapons. Again, I would say there was enough for easily one per man. This large group of people were drinking beer, cans and bottles. They were very joyful. They were waving the weapons in the air as if to toast, as if to be happy with what was happening at that moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What kind of impression did you have as regards these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't call them soldiers, for a start. I'd call them, what I would say was a -- I put one and one together. I just saw the scenes of passing through the village. These people now are less than 400, 500 metres, if that, away from what all was happening, so that they couldn't hear what was happening, if they weren't responsible, which I doubt, then I just -- I don't know. I would like to say. At that moment in time, just -- I turned, I traversed the gun of the tank, which is a 30-millimetre gun, towards these people, and -- well -- I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I will ask the usher to show you Exhibit 119. You didn't take this picture yourself, so please just identify the building which is behind the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is what we call the Swiss chalet. It's off the bend to the left-hand side of the road with, as we can see, a large forecourt patio area which is where the all these soldiers were stood, about this area with all their weapons, toasting and cheering with the beer, and the turnaround point as we are looking at the picture is off to the right-hand side on the other side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you saw these people for the first time, these soldiers, you were driving toward Zenica, weren't you? And can you show us on the aerial photograph behind you which route you followed, and where you turned round?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was driving down the main road. This place here, known as the Bungalow on the map is where the Swiss chalet is, and the turn-around point is just off the map to the large -- it used to be a grassed area but it's worn out. We used to use it a lot to turn around when we were on road routes. It was a common turn around point that we used to use. It's dried-up mud, off the main road. As we are looking at this map, to the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It's on your way back to Ahmici that you targeted these men with your gun?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, targeted -- I wouldn't say targeted. Targeted is when you want to shoot. I didn't shoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Why did you do that? What was the significance of this?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I aimed my gun at them because of anger, again because like I said, I put what I saw to what I'm looking at at that present point in time, these people, not soldiers, as to what I had saw, and I put one and one together as to what I thought; they had done the scenes that I had just seen. I didn't operate a trigger as such or anything because I believe that -- well, discipline, amongst other things, took over, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you were saying they were not soldiers, are you saying that they were not people who had the moral qualities of a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: In my eyes sir, correct, yes sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And according to you, they didn't have these qualities because, in your mind, they were associated to the incidents you had witnessed in Ahmici before; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you describe the rest of your travel, of your route?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As I said, we've turned around now, we've aimed our gun at these people, we've now forgot that incident as such and we've drove off, back slowly again, up the road negotiated the bend to again where these people were on now the right-hand side of the road because we're driving back towards Vitez, told these people again just to wait. We carried on, looked at the map, and on the vehicles we have, on the Warriors, we have what's called a navigational system which pinpoints exactly where you are with satellites, basically. I looked at this and realised my grid was on to my left-hand side, looked at the map, found the road that I wanted, which is the road here, and we drove up that road in a northerly direction, nice and slow again up the road to notice that on the right again were houses burning and destroyed and on the left-hand side of the road there's now a lot of cattle in the area which was dead. It had been shot. We carried on up the road until we went past the mosque up to this area here. All this area now to me was new. I had never been up this road before on this tour of Bosnia. We looked to the right and we saw the broken-down Scimitar which was there with the other vehicle. We talked to the driver on the radio, talked to him through word of mouth because his radio wasn't working, shouting at him, to find that the vehicle in front had broken down. The other vehicle was just behind. That was okay. So we negotiated and turned around to face back down the track facing towards the cow field, this way here. Once the REME vehicle went in to the Scimitar and carried on fixing it, we could hear, not very loudly because the engine and the noise of the vehicles, but behind us there was gunfire, just a single gun, the same gun. And as we looked through our sights down towards the field which I've pointed out, we could see cattle being shot at, and there was one specific cow which was being shot, kept falling down, getting back up as it was shot at again, and this was repeatedly happening until the cattle stayed down. We thought the gunfire was coming from behind us. With the engine noise, we couldn't exactly make out where it was coming from. As this was going on, the REME had got in touch with me from their vehicle to say that the vehicle was not fixable, so they connected it up to their vehicle and we led our way back then to the garage, back down the way we came, back down the track, turning right at the end, and heading back towards the garage and the order, I led the way, followed by the broken -- followed by the REME vehicle towing the broken-down vehicle and the other Scimitar behind. We got back to the garage. We left all those vehicles there, the three of them, and I then reported back to my Ops room in the school to tell them that -- the job we had just done, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you talk about your second journey to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: When I got back to the Ops room after this first one, I said to the people in the Ops room what I've just seen down in the village, and I told them that I had given some instructions out to these four women and child to stay there for ten minutes 'cause I'll be back. I got told at that point that I couldn't go back, but I informed the person I was speaking to that I had to go back because I've given my word, so I went back to the park, got in my vehicle, and got one of my other vehicles with me, which is call sign 3-2. We then drove back at great speed to Ahmici, to the exact point where these people were inside or behind this mud bank covered with leaves. We stopped, he stayed a distance behind, and we opened the back doors and we started loading these people on. The vehicle I had, which is a -- it's a command variant which means it's got two back doors and there's space inside -- it's only got four chairs. You could get, I suppose, two people up on one of these chairs and two tables and they collapse down. At this point, though, lots of women came running from this mud bank and got into the back of the vehicle. When they all got into the back of the vehicle, we closed the door, had a quick count to find out there was 13 women, two children. We gave them some hot drink and some biscuits which we always carry on board, in a kettle, I suppose you could call it. As this was happening, I then looked behind me and saw the other vehicle, 3-2, reversed round to face back up towards the north, this way, and what he was doing was the same. People were coming from one of the houses and they were then getting on board his vehicle with lots of belongings. As this was happening, off to the right-hand side there's like a fenced-off area, which is like a builder's merchant's yard, as such. A man was on the inside and he was pulling at the gate to try to get out but the gate had a chain and padlock on it, so the gate was only open a small amount of the way. He couldn't get out so he dropped to the ground quickly, shuffled underneath, and ran towards the vehicle. I didn't open the doors at this point because I didn't know who he was. As he got towards the back door, we could see he had no weapons on him and he was in complete civilian clothes and he was very frightened. We opened the doors and he got into the back of our vehicle. At this point I then took another photograph looking out of the back of the vehicle, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like the usher to show you Exhibit number 245. Did you take this picture?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Was this photograph taken when the incidents you've just mentioned took place, when the civilians embarked into your vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you describe the vehicle in the middle of the photograph? What is it doing now?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: The vehicle here, is what's known as traversing, in other words, it doesn't move as such, the wheels don't go round. All it does is spin on its axis and it's spinning to the left to move forward and reverse up to allow these people here to get into the back of the vehicle, and as you can see it's taken from a vehicle, this is an antenna and these here are the back bins, as we call them, on a vehicle, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At that moment there are two vehicles on the road, the one we can see and yours, where the picture is taken from.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: This picture is taken from the back of my vehicle as I'm looking backwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where this young man was coming from, who arrived at the last minute?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Here, sir, from this area, from this fenced-off area here, which was like -- it was like a builder's merchant's -- bits of wood, planks of wood. Just back from it, you can't see it, in this direction, along here, further back, there's like a shed which had no frontage to it and all the wood, bricks, and sand and whatever, bits and bobs, they were all in that area there, so we called it a builder's -- a merchant yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How did he manage to jump the fence that we can see in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Can you repeat that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How this young man managed to jump the fence that we can see on the right-hand side of the photograph, to go over it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: He didn't jump the fence. He tried to open the fence but it wouldn't open because there's a chain and a padlock on it. What he done was dropped on his belly, crawled underneath the gate, and got up and ran towards the vehicle this way here (indicating), sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In which vehicle did he embark? On the one we see on your photograph or in your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: In my vehicle, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What did you do afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Once this was finished, then the other vehicle now was facing back up the road towards Vitez. We then neutral turned our vehicle to face the same way, and I talked on the radio to the vehicle behind, and we made our way at best speed up to Travnik hospital. We drove all the way to Travnik hospital, which was on the right-hand side of the road, went under like a large verandah, entranceway, got into the hospital forecourt, car park area where a lot of nurses came rushing out with trolleys, like stretchers on them. We then disembarked the people from the vehicle. There was a very, very old woman, I mean grandmother age, so to speak. We then got out of the vehicle, we all got out of the vehicle, and she then embraced me, gave me a hug, and she was talking to the nurses, and she wouldn't let me go. She was trembling, as was the same with the rest of them. She then was taken away by the doctors, and they all went into the hospital, and that's the last we heard of them, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: During the journey in Ahmici in April 1993, did you have the feeling that there was a battle going on between various armed groups?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, sir. There was no -- there was no two sides there, there was only this one amount of people and they were at the Swiss chalet. There was no sort of anything around the area to say that there was a battle in that area. No, I suppose you'd call it, defences. There was nothing like that in the area, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If we exclude these people you saw at the Swiss cottage. Did you see in Ahmici men wearing uniforms and weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, sir, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In the days following, or in the weeks following, the day of the 16th of April, 1993, did you go back to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, sir. When Ahmici then became public, I suppose, lots of visits were made back there with lots of press, et cetera, and I did go back only the one time, which was well after some bodies had been found in a burnt-out cellar which was the only time -- but that was weeks later, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please indicate on this photograph, using one of the pens you have just in front of you, the place where this young man managed to embark in your vehicle? Where he managed to crawl under the fence, to be more precise. Put an X, for instance. You've got some pens on your desk.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: There, sir. (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question. On the aerial photograph which is just behind you, can you tell us where you took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believed up until I've been here for the last two days, sir, that I took this photograph here, but I've now been informed that it was here, sir (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: To explain this last evidence from the witness, I would like to say that this witness has already testified in the Blaskic case, and in the Blaskic case, the witness described the same scene which we can see on the photograph. However, he told the Court that this picture had been taken further away down the road in another bend. We talked about it when we met, and since there is no doubt about the place where the picture was taken because you can realise this when you see the picture. I noticed that maybe in the Blaskic case and during his testimony there was a little bit of confusion since these events took place a long time ago, but just to make things clear, there can be no doubt as far as the place where the picture was taken is concerned and as far as the place where this incident took place is concerned. I have no further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness will be cross-examined by Defence counsel Susak and then Counsel Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: We are going to speak now about the photograph 245. Could you tell us, where were you standing when you saw this person which, as you said, crawled from beneath the fence?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: As I mentioned, sir, in my vehicle, it is -- I'm in the turret of the vehicle here -- sorry, here. Basically I'm on the left-hand side and I'm turned around so I'm facing back towards Vitez way. I'm on the left-hand side and the gunner is on the right-hand side and I'm looking through the back centre of the vehicle up here at the top. We can just see where the hatch has sprung open and it stays in that position, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Can you indicate with a cross the place where -- this place, where you were or where your vehicle was?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Indicate where -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that you were in the turret. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? Could you tell us where exactly you were at that moment with the pointer? I'm referring to the vehicle. You were on the left side in the vehicle, you said.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Okay sir. Sorry. If we look at the vehicle behind, we see the main hull, which is the bottom part of the vehicle, and we can see the top part, which is the turret. Here now where I'm pointing is a silhouette of a person. That there is the commander. He is on the right-hand side as the vehicle faces forward. I am in that position but on this front vehicle, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Can you indicate where this front vehicle is?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Here, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you indicate with a cross the part of the vehicle where you were sitting or standing at that moment?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Indicate on the rear vehicle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I imagine so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't quite understand the question, but if the witness understood the question, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could he put a circle around the place where he was sitting, not a cross, so there is no confusion.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I'm on the front vehicle, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Would you indicate where the front vehicle was at that moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Where should he indicate this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am interested in the angle of the vehicle, whether the witness could see this scene from that angle, because if he was in the turret, I believe that under a certain angle, he couldn't see the lower part of the fence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: He took this photograph --

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I took this photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This was taken by the witness. So if he was able to take this photograph covering also the fence, that means that he was able to see the fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked him where he was at the point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You did not ask him where he was. It was made quite plain that he is the photographer. You then asked him to fill in on that photograph, which shows the other tank, where it was that he was sitting. So what he filled in was the equivalent position. You've caused total confusion. He was the photographer. This is what he saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, Judge May, where was he when he saw the man coming out of the courtyard from under the fence? To tell me where he was, what his position was at that time, moment.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. I am the camera. That is my view of what I can see obviously with a wider scope. That is the lens. I can see that plus more of what you can see now with the photograph, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Can you indicate approximately the place, the location where you were, or the direction?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, okay. This here -- this here, this thing sticking up, is the rear of my vehicle and it's an antenna which goes up when we're stationary. This line and this one here, a shadow, are rear bins of the vehicle, and in between that, what you can't see here, are these two opening back doors. That is the rear of my vehicle. That there is my hat -- sorry, the gunner's hatch, I'm on the left-hand side, the whole vehicle is facing forward but I, as you can see, I've taken the photograph, facing the rear -- the turret is still facing forward, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Were you in the vehicle or were you on the road, on the asphalt?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: In the vehicle, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: That's what I was asking you. Were you in the turret of the vehicle? Were you in the turret of that vehicle? Could you describe the place where you were situated in the vehicle, your place in the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. As the vehicle is facing forward, as this vehicle here that I'm pointing out is, I am on the front right of that vehicle as the commander. The gunner is the front left person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you draw an arrow showing what is rear and what is front for you. What, according to you, is rear and what is front?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: (Marks). A is rear and B is front, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So you are looking towards the width of the road. Could you put the longitudinal in the longitudinal, what is front and what is rear, with an arrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: The direction of the road. Your Honour, the witness is saying that he is looking at the front, the longitudinal axis with an arrow, as regards the longitudinal axis of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't really understand.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: This is towards Vitez, that way, and the other area towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: This is not clear again. I asked you to draw only one arrow which will indicate the direction, what is front, and you put two arrows. Now I don't know what is rear, what is front?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You put one arrow and a "V," namely Vitez. This is what you did.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There is one arrow pointing toward the other tank and a "V" meaning Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have understood now. I thought the "V" was an arrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Please, could we avoid putting more marks on this photograph because otherwise you won't understand a thing using this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: At what moment did you see that person in the fence or within the fence, within the area of the fence? At what point did you see him or where was the person when you saw him for the first time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: My vehicle -- on this photograph now, my vehicle is loaded up with the 13 women and two children. The man is also on the vehicle as the photograph was taken. The man came from behind this gate here, underneath it, and around this way. Afterwards, which is when this photograph was taken, this vehicle is manoeuvring to load these people up here, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You hadn't answered my question. I said, when did you first see that person? I'm not talking about the movement, I am asking you when did you first see him, at what place -- in what place? What was the position?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I first saw the person --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you see him coming out of the fence or crawling under the fence or crossing -- jumping over the fence?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I think I've already said that he was on the other side of the fence, he attempted to open the gate, he couldn't, because it was chained, so he dropped to the ground, crawled under, and then ran to the vehicle, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: ... saw him the first time under the fence? Within the fence?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: The first time I saw him was on the inside of the compound, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: How -- what was the distance between the person and the fence?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Inches, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Metres, inches?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Inches. He was trying to get out. He was pulling the gate to get out but couldn't get out so he then dropped to the ground and went underneath, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I'm concluding that you saw him at the gate. I asked you how -- what was the distance between him and the gate when you first saw him? Can you say that? Your Honour, you will probably understand better if we say -- if we show the witness the aerial photograph 247 where the courtyard and the building and the fence are seen. You will then understand my question. Could you please say in this photograph, when did you first see this person? What was the exact point? Could you put a cross there? You see the fence now. You can see the fence now.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yeah, I can see the fence, but it doesn't -- this gate is on the roadside. That gate there is on another side. It's a different photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I want this photograph to be left there. Could you indicate with an arrow the open gate or with a circle?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: The gate's not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: There is no gate, Mr. President, on this photograph. This is not the same view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: This is the same view. This is the same photograph. It is an exhibit. And it shows that the gate is open. I want the witness to encircle the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this photograph -- it goes back to March 1998, this photograph. It was not taken by the witness and we can see that on the road there is no gate, and that the gate which is shown on picture 245 is not visible on this particular picture. It's probably not the same portion of road on Exhibit 245 and on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Counsel Susak, can you see?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: ... want the witness to encircle the place where the person was when he first saw him because the witness said that a person crawled from beneath the fence onto the road. I would like him -- the witness to encircle the place where this person was when he saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The photograph that is visible now is completely different. First of all, the buildings weren't there. They look like concrete. It was a wooden building with an open front. The gates, as we can see, are there. They weren't. I'd guess that they were on this side here -- not a guess. They were on this side here. So it's completely different. I can't mark where he was, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: But in this direction you can see the building. Keep to the direction of the building. Or if you can't mark it, could you tell us how far the person was from the wire fence when you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Susak, you are asking again and again the same question. I wonder whether you could move on to your next question because you asked this question many times and now the witness can't identify on this picture the gate, so let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Will you. Will you then tell us how that individual was dressed, the one that ran to your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, he was dressed in civilian clothes. There was no military clothing about him whatsoever, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: While he was within the fence, did he shout to you, did he communicate with you verbally?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, sir. As again I've said, all we done was seen him trying to get under the fence. He didn't communicate in any way. He didn't have to. The look on his face when he got close to us was enough. We could see that he was trying to get out of that building in somewhat of a scared manner. He was trying to get out. He attempted the gates, couldn't get out, so he quickly dropped to the ground, belly-crawled underneath the gates, and then ran to the vehicle where again, as we've said, we looked at him, identified that he had no weapons about him, he had no military clothing whatsoever, so we opened the back doors and inside, and in our vehicle he got, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Since he crawled under the fence, did you then measure the distance between -- the gap between the ground and the fence? Did you happen to notice that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, sir, but it was big enough for him to get under and crawl.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Right. From the distance, how could you see that the gate was padlocked?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Because he attempted to pull it. He attempted to pull the gate, it wouldn't open -- well, it opened a couple of millimetres, inches, centimetres, whatever you want to call it, it opened a little bit, but he couldn't get out, so he dropped to the ground and went underneath it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did he get through immediately or did he wait for a while?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, sir, straightaway he dropped to the ground and straight underneath. Straightaway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So without any obstacle. All right. You say that -- you cannot indicate the place you say you saw him first. But do you know -- do you know what his function at that facility was?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Do you mean what his job was?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. What was his job there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. Don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you describe that person, what he looks like, how tall he is, whether he was wearing a cap?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, couldn't describe anything. It's five years ago. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: But you remember what was happening in the Bungalow five years ago.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: In the Bungalow with all the men? In the chalet?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes. You remember what was there, and here you can't remember.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Well, because that was the largest mass of men I had seen to that date. I had never seen a hundred men in Bosnia in military clothes with lots of weapons, never, until that day. That's why that sticks in my head. But I saw lots of people on the road and I can't remember this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you know how this man happened to be inside the fence and where he was before that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: All right. Did you see this man standing in front of the fence, or was he moving?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: He was on the inside of the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I'll ask you, was he standing or was he moving when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: He was trying to open the gate. He was moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Lordship. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kujawinski. I will ask you some questions related to your first tour of Ahmici. Could you tell us what time it was? At about what time did you set out? You said after 2.00, but could you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Certainly. According to the notes I have or had, it was about 14.40 hours, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And some place in Ahmici or, rather, you reached a bungalow. How long did it take you to get to the Bungalow, roughly? Half an hour? An hour?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I suppose between 15 minutes and half an hour, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, those bodies you saw on the left-hand side of the road when you showed it you said that -- you showed us on the map and said they were mostly on the left side of the road. How many bodies were there again, roughly, if you could tell us?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I've said in the formal statement when I was on the -- in the box last time that I saw approximately 13 up that road, i.e. here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You counted them? You counted those bodies?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't count them individually, no, but I'm guessing there was about 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So this one vehicle had broken down in Ahmici, the one that they had reported and asked you to drag it away. But were the bodies collected in Ahmici before you turned up there? Did UNPROFOR members collect those bodies; would you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Not myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And those soldiers you saw in front of the Bungalow, you said they were wearing dark uniforms; is that so? Were they black uniforms or what? What does "dark" mean?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: As I said before, they weren't black and they weren't -- they were like a dark, very, very dark in colour. Again, to that date we had seen very, very dark camouflage green and we had also seen completely black uniforms. It was just like a whole array or mixture of very dark uniforms, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So they were of both kinds, they were dark green, dark camouflage, dark ...

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Just very dark, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You are familiar with the HVO patch, aren't you, with HVO insignia? You used to see it. You know. You know what the HVO insignia looks like, the ones that the ordinary soldiers, that the privates wore on their sleeves. Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I know the Croat symbol and the Muslim symbol, I know both symbols. Again, we were shown many, many books -- distinct ones, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And such a symbol, and this symbol you did not see on the sleeve of soldiers who were at this Swiss chalet because you are familiar with that particular symbol?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I only saw -- I only recall seeing this one specific patch that day or that time, should I say, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And it was not the usual HVO symbol, was it? That insignia that you saw on that occasion, you don't remember ever seeing it again?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No. The only symbol I saw that day was, as I said, was a shield, red, white, blue from left to right going vertical with an arch across the top of it, but I don't know what it was. Don't know, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see some lettering on that patch, on that insignia? Were there any letters? Did you see them?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No. Last time I came, I was shown an A4 file with many, many, many pages of different patches to try and get my head going but, no, it didn't work. There was no writing on it. There was nothing. I couldn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You're referring to General Blaskic's trial, is it, the last time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Right. You also testified that you did not see soldiers with rifles in the village, so you did not see any soldiers with rifles in the village, either those belonging to the army of B and H or the HVO, in Ahmici itself you did not see soldiers with rifles?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, I saw nobody in the village whatsoever, only on that drive past when there was people dead on the side and we picked those people up and the only two male people I seen was the one we picked up and the one in the house and obviously all of the soldiers down at the Swiss chalet. Otherwise, no soldiers whatsoever in the village, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The second time you came to Ahmici, when was that, approximately? When you returned; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: The second time that day?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: That specific day? Well, I had to go to the garage to drop off the broken-down vehicle, to go back to the school, have a discussion, brief up people, and then go back up. I guess now about maybe just short of an hour or just over an hour, somewhere around there, ma'am? A guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So around 5.00? Around 5.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I wouldn't put a time on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was it getting dark?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, it wasn't getting dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you still hear shots in the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, not when we went back. No, there was nothing. The only shots in the village were that one time and that was way off to the left and that was just an individual, that was. It wasn't a battle or anything as such. It was just a -- one man far away shooting at this cattle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But when you arrived the first time, you could hear fire?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yeah, when we got to the broken-down vehicle. We couldn't hear it from the roadside. But when we got to the broken-down vehicle and turned around, that's when we could hear it. It's hard to hear with the engine on, but you could hear a very distinct crack of a rifle, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Right. Let me just go back. You kept telling us about those bodies on the left side of the road and that house by the cemetery where you say you saw two bodies. Were there any other bodies near the Catholic cemetery that you might remember? It is on the right-hand side of the road.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No. Again, from memory, not that I remember, but if I remember right, the Catholic cemetery -- well, as we can see, is on the bend, but the Catholic cemetery is high. It's on like a hill, a small hill or, shall we say, the ground on the right is high and this drops away so you can't exactly see into the cemetery clearly 'cause it's very high, the cemetery, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I mean within the boundaries of the cemetery, I mean to the side of the cemetery or near the cemetery, on the other side; you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: On the right-hand side of the road, all I remember is there wasn't much destruction or much -- many bodies there, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You spoke about yet another event which you witnessed in April 1993. You said you were at a locality called Miletici on the 20th of April, 1993. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this question. I didn't mention, during my questioning, the events at Miletici. I don't think the questions are justified just to check the credibility of the witness. Of course, I know that this Tribunal can allow this; however, there is no direct relationship between the indictment and Miletici but, of course, it's up to you to decide on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Your Lordship, may I say something, respond to this objection? The question of Miletici was already raised before when some other witnesses appeared and certain things -- I don't know. Sometimes the Prosecution goes beyond the boundaries of the indictment and I do not see why can't we do it if we have a truthful witness because otherwise we shall have to ask for this witness to come and testify again and we do not think it would really be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have Rule 90(H), whereby cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of the direct examination matters affecting the credibility of the witness. The Trial Chamber may, in the exercise of its discretion, permit inquiry into additional matters as if on direct examination. We have decided you may go on and ask questions about Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, you were in Miletici on two occasions. Could you tell us where that village is and who you went with there? I am referring to the 27th of April, 1994 -- '93?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: We got again tasked by the Ops room to go to Miletici to -- we were informed that there was a disturbance in that area. We weren't told what the disturbance was. So I was dispatched with two vehicles, two Warriors, and a UNHCR Land Rover and occupants to find out if food was getting through, I think -- I think. We navigated our way there. It's very north from Vitez. It's down towards the Travnik -- it's on the Travnik road from Vitez but then it's off to the right, up through the mountains and the mountain pass, so to speak. It's right in the hills off to the right-hand side as you're driving north. It's a tiny little village, was -- it was very peaceful, so I could imagine it was. As we got to the base of the hill, the track was very, very thin, and there was no way -- we thought there was no way we were going to get a Warrior vehicle up the track, so we got some of the way by taking out the side of a hedge, and then I told one of the vehicles, one of the Warriors to stay there. I then debussed, that is got out of the vehicle, and walked the vehicle, that is commanded it from the ground up the hill to make sure it wasn't going to go over. We went up this hill followed by the Land Rover and the other Warrior stayed some way down the bottom. We got to the actual village where it was, and it was a very, very small village of which I do have photographs again -- I don't know if there is any exhibits here, whatever. It's a very small forecourt in the centre of the village and to the right-hand side there was a distinctive, what looked like pink house and houses around to the right. Straight on, it was like the front end of a house looking at us, the door end, and off to the left there was an old ruin just down off the side of a drop, which is all knocked down, very old building. When we got up there, through the interpreter with the UNHCR lady, she started asking the people if everything was okay and what was going on in the area, to find out that everything wasn't okay, but they wouldn't let us go near this pink house, as such. Soldiers being soldiers what we are, we got out and had a look around the area while the interpreter carried on talking to her. As we walked around the building we could see there was old blood, dried blood on the floor by the entrance to the house. We asked in the village what had gone on, through the interpreter again, and they were saying, "Nothing, nothing." So in the end, one of them told the interpreter that some soldiers -- she didn't name the soldiers to begin with -- had come to the village and had rounded up everybody who was in the village, took them into this old ruin which didn't have a roof or anything, and these soldiers then had segregated the people from fighting people into non-fighting people. With that, they were left with several young men who could have been soldiers according to their knowledge, I suppose. What happened then was they let them go but they took these people who they thought could have been soldiers into this pink house, and in this house again she told us that they had done things to them, and that was as far as it went. The night was closing in now and we talked to this woman repeatedly trying to get into the house and it had come round again through the interpreter that we had found out now that these men had been killed in this house. Not how and where they were now, she wouldn't tell us none of that, but -- what we then said to her, we will get these people buried. We will bury your people now --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How many people were involved?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: In the killings?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did they say what people they were? Did they mention anyone? Did they just say who those people might be because Mujahedeen were mentioned in the -- during the investigation. But was there any mention of who those people might be?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: There was, but not at this point -- I mean, we didn't even know at this point how many people there was. She wouldn't tell us anything. But again through this interpreter we found out --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You didn't really understand my meaning. I'm asking about the perpetrators, I mean, about those responsible for it. What did the villagers tell you who had done that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: At this point now as where I am in my story, I suppose, they hadn't told us how many people had been killed or who had killed them. They just said soldiers had been there. They didn't tell us anything. Eventually we got into this house, this pink house, and there was blood, really dark red blood scattered amongst the walls. There was pillows which had been used to muffle shots, we think. Feathers everywhere. There was a settee covered in flood, and on the floor and walls there was like clots of hair and bone just strewn on the walls and it looked like someone had marked down with a hand. At this point now she now told us that there was five of them, all in all, who had been, she said, tortured in this house, and the evidence before us looked like that as well. We said to her, you know, that if you tell us where they are, et cetera, then we could bury them for you, and we never did that day. It was getting dark now, and a villager, one man, came to us and said that loads of soldiers were on the way, and at this time we said, "Well, what do you mean? How many soldiers?" He said lots of soldiers now travelling from the south to the north, the route that we just took, and they were coming up this way, so to speak. We immediately said to her, we'll be back tomorrow. We'll go in. And with that we left rather rapid. We got down to the very bottom of the road after passing our other vehicle to find out we had actually bumped into these soldiers and these were all Muslim soldiers in lots of transport and this now goes on from what I said that this now is the largest number of soldiers I've seen. There was --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The second largest group of soldiers that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, according to Ahmici, and there was, I guess, 200 plus in different types of vehicles, old dump trucks, buses, vans, all sorts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Armed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: All mixed. All mixed up. All in different types of uniforms, civilians, et cetera. Very cheerful, very jolly, didn't -- you know, just talked to us normal. Didn't do anything. And they were making their way north. Now, at that point the border between the Serbs and the Croats was very close and the Bosnians were very close, it was literally two k's up that road, and that was where they were going. We said hello, they said hello. A quick chat and then we shot off back to our Ops. It was very dark now, very dark. We got to our Ops room, told them exactly what we had seen, soldiers going up, the village, et cetera. The next day we returned very early to that village with exactly the same people plus a lorry known as a Bedford, we call it, which is a troop transporter, and in that troop transport we carried coffins. We got the coffins from Vitez, from a timber -- a big massive timber yard just further down from the school, and we put the coffins on board. We also put crosses on board. And we then drove off to Miletici again, same route, exactly the same thing, got up to the top, met these people again, started talking. Again, they weren't going to hand over the bodies. We had a guy called ... Steve Arthur, Company Sergeant Major Arthur, he had a separate interpreter on his own, he negotiated, and eventually they told us these bodies were in the house opposite, with the front door shown to us. This again took a while that day and the bodies were then placed into coffins. I took the names on a notebook. The names are inscribed on these crosses. And we then took the coffins to -- I think it's Gora Guce, I think it's called.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: To Guca Gora, we took the bodies there. When we got there, a very nice old church. We met a monk. We handed over the bodies. The graves were already dug. How he knew -- just anticipating. We handed over the bodies. I do remember at that point that there was lots of Croat flags in the area all hanging from lamp posts and everything in that village. We then handed over the bodies, turned around, and went back. I don't know what time that was, though, at that point, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, in what state were the bodies? Could you see that these people had been tortured? What did they look like?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: It was obvious that the bodies had been in this room for several days 'cause when we opened the door, the door closed itself behind us. It was disgusting. The bodies, as they were laid out, one was very, very bloated, you know, not naturally fat, just built up with gases. Another guy, his neck was just barely hanging on. It had been cut all the way around with what can only be described as a blunt instrument. It was just cut all the way around. Another body, his fingers were bent backwards all the way backwards from the direction that they're supposed to bend.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And the bodies were dead, had been dead for some time, according to -- in your judgement?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. In my judgement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What information did you get? Who did it? What did the people in the village tell you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I think it was on that second day now, early when we got there, we carried on the negotiations. They saw that we brought the coffins and we were willing to help. They told us that Mujahedin had actually been to that area and had done that. They said it was people they had not seen before, never saw them before, and they actually said the words it was Mujahedin had been in that area, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, did they tell you that part of the people were driven out of the village? Did you see men in the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: We did see men in the village but again, as I said at the beginning, they were very, very old men not fighting age men. The only fighting men were those dead five people. Everyone else was gone from the village that could fight.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you hear about these people being expelled from the village, driven out of the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, ma'am, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'll have some very short questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about these 200 Muslim soldiers that you saw when you left Miletici to go back to Vitez. Can you tell us on what day this happened?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Late April. I think -- I think -- I think of it was the 24th of April. I'm not sure. I'm not sure now, sir. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think Mrs. Glumac said 27th of April. The first day was the 27th of April, is what you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The 26th, the first day, the 27th the second day. These are the gentleman's notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And I agree with Mrs. Glumac's notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Where were these soldiers going to? In which direction?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: They were travelling north up the valley towards the border, the then border.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At that time you were talking about a frontline with the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At that time where was this frontline?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: From the point where we were, where we turned off to go up to Miletici, which was on a very sharp S-bend, first bend into the right, it was approximately 2 kilometres north.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As far as the atrocities that you saw in Miletici, did you learn when these atrocities took place?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, sir, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We were wondering if it would be possible to know where Miletici is, precisely. Is it far away from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: If I could give directions? Reference to Ahmici, if you go down the road towards Vitez, on the road to Travnik you come to basically one prominent turn off to the right which is going into the valleys. You follow that road all the way up -- there's only one road. It's a main drag, so to speak. You drive all the way up there and it's off to your right in the hills, very high in the hills.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: How far away from Ahmici, roughly speaking? So how many kilometres? Ten? Twenty? Anyway, we will ...

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I'd say about 15 to 20, I'd say, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I see there are no further questions? There are no questions. Thank you, Sergeant, for coming here to give evidence in court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I suggest we now take a break and reconvene in half an hour, should we say at twenty past four, for the Status Conference? Are you going to formally close your case? You are not going to make a final statement, or are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I won't give any final statement. We don't have other witnesses at this stage. However, but we can talk about it when we come back, I will have a certain number of documents to tender; for instance, we will have a certain number of death certificates and other useful documents as well. Maybe we could discuss the way these documents should be tendered into evidence. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So it won't take more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, I'd say fifteen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Okay. Fifteen. Then we will resume the hearing at twenty past. First of all we will receive these documents and see if they can be tendered into evidence and then we will do the Status Conference. Would you like this conference to be a closed hearing? No? All right. So we will rise now until twenty past four.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The first document we would like to tender relates to death certificates. Various elements of the indictment require that we bring evidence in front of you that some people died during the events. We have already handed to the Tribunal a certain number of elements that we gathered through testimonies, we have already handed in a certain number of documents which show that there were 104 murders during the events that relate to the accused. So the figure is 104 plus a certain number of refugees who died on the very same day at Ahmici. Today we would like to hand to the Tribunal and tender into evidence 93 death certificates. These certificates were established by the administrative services of the Vitez municipality, that is, the service that was to register the births and deaths of people over a certain territory. They were transmitted to us by these services and relate to people who died either on the 16th of April or the 17th of April, 1993. Of course, maybe in the rebuttal case we would call a representative of the Vitez municipality who could offer these documents through his testimony, but we think it would be simpler and more efficient to present these documents following this procedure. If their authenticity was to be contested, if their origin was to be discussed, of course we would ask for one of these witnesses to be called during our rebuttal case. However, we think that the Tribunal may find useful these death certificates as of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Lordships, we object to the inclusion of these documents in the case records as evidence. It is quite true that the Prosecution submitted death certificates. The death certificates for individual persons may be admitted only for persons identified at the burial but not death certificates issued for persons not identified during the burial or whose body is missing. In the territory of the former Yugoslavia and in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for persons, if we use the Western vocabulary, are missing, there is a special procedure conducive to the establishment or the ascertainment of one's death. We should therefore like to have admitted into evidence death certificates only for those persons of whom we are certain that they are dead; and for persons that this has not been established, we cannot accept them because there is no manner in which one can ascertain that a certain person is indeed dead.
